items.stem: Which set best captures the five objectives of high-velocity IT?

options.text: Valuable, fast, resilient, co-created, and assured investments/services
options.rationale: Correct: HVIT aims for valuable, fast, resilient, co-created and assured outcomes.

options.text: Cheap, outsourced, documented, approved and audited
options.rationale: These are not the HVIT objectives.

options.text: Manual, controlled, infrequent, centralised and fixed
Scoped, chartered, funded, staffed and closed
options.rationale: These are generic project stages, not HVIT objectives.

items.explanation: Correct: HVIT aims for valuable, fast, resilient, co-created and assured outcomes.

items.stem: A team automates its release pipeline and adds automated tests to catch defects earlier. Which HVIT objective is most directly supported?

options.text: Fast (and resilient) delivery through earlier feedback
options.rationale: Correct: automation and early testing shorten feedback loops, supporting fast and resilient delivery.
Co-creation is about collaboration with consumers, not the pipeline automation itself.
Compliance may benefit, but the primary effect is faster, more resilient delivery.
Automation is central to HVIT practices and objectives.

items.explanation: Correct: automation and early testing shorten feedback loops, supporting fast and resilient delivery.

items.stem: Which TWO ITIL guiding principles are especially emphasised in high-velocity IT?

options.rationale: Correct: iterating with feedback is central to high-velocity working.
Correct: optimising then automating is key to achieving velocity.
This is not a guiding principle and conflicts with iterative delivery.
Centralising decisions is not a guiding principle and slows flow.
Managing risk, not avoiding all of it, is the aim.

items.explanation: Correct: iterating with feedback is central to high-velocity working.
